A bloody, muscular, barrelhouse of a vampire movie that throbs like the neck of a blues guitar on fire, Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners” might be the first story the “Creed” director has ripped straight from his own guts.
With “Sinners,” an inimitable auteur makes the most of every surrealist detail and crafts a fright fest that’s musical and meaningful, mesmerizing and memorable.
Sinners marks another strong reason why Ryan Coogler is at the top of his generation of filmmakers, and Jordan continues to show why he is a real deal movie star.
Although sometimes a little overstuffed, the picture consistently gets under the skin thanks to its expertly-staged fright sequences that reverberate with insidious societal ills.
Much like the vampires it depicts, Coogler’s latest shall be immortal. Sinners is a timeless tale that is part social commentary, part creature feature, and a boldly bloody good time.

As much arthouse as grindhouse, it’s a blood-drenched mix tape that shouldn’t work. But it does, thanks to Coogler’s muscular direction, a terrific cast, enveloping IMAX visuals, body-quaking sound and music that stirs the soul.
Part-Southern gothic nightmare, part-rock ‘n’ roll opera, Sinners is the rare film that possesses you body and soul.

It’s surprising that it holds together, given the sheer number of tones on display. What’s practically a miracle, however, is that it’s also one of 2025’s most sharply conceived works of popcorn entertainment.
With Sinners, Ryan Coogler confirms that he has a real talent for exploring and reinventing genres, while still telling a story that feels wholly original.
Sinners works more than it doesn’t, even if it doesn’t always gel, but it’s a commanding demonstration of how lavishly spirited and “serious” a popcorn movie can be.
The way Coogler resolves Sinners’ central ideas within a traditional horror-story framework is truly masterful.
Stunningly photographed, engrossing cinema — epic to the point where it seemingly never ends, which is undeniably indulgent, but no great sin.

Stylish, sexy, scary, and full of horror violence, Sinners is a wild feature with plenty on its mind, further showing what Coogler can accomplish at the height of his powers. However, I’m not even convinced that he’s reached the peak of his capabilities.
We simply don't get original blockbusters with this level of passion and on this scale anymore, at least outside of a Christopher Nolan or M. Night Shyamalan production.
It’s rare to see a big studio film where the director has been given freedom to fully realize his period setting at the expense of the plot.
Sinners is a bloody, action-packed, medium scary horror that's dripping with cultural flavor. This could be one of Ryan Coogler's best films to date.
